questions.knowledge_point: Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of Y
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093736/assets/22328ca144ecfaf7c1d52abd77c59f03dbf3c0da36fff21a809ce4e456ed56a5.png)

Consider the arc of the curve $x={y}^{3}-9y$ that lies in the fourth quadrant between its $y$-intercepts. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{3}-9y & =0 \\ y({y}^{2}-9) & =0 \\ y & =0,\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $y=-3$ to $y=0.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3}-9y)=3{y}^{2}-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-3}^{0}({y}^{3}-9y)\sqrt{1+(3{y}^{2}-9)^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-3}^{0}({y}^{3}-9y)\sqrt{1+9({y}^{2}-3)^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $x=\sqrt{y-3}$ that lies between the lines $y=3$ and $y=\frac{15}{4}.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\sqrt{y-3})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y-3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}=\frac{1}{4(y-3)}.
$$

Then, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{3}^{15/4}\sqrt{y-3}\cdot \sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4(y-3)}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{3}^{15/4}\sqrt{y-3}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{4y-11}{4(y-3)}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{3}^{15/4}\sqrt{4y-11}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=4y-11.$ Then, $\text{d}y=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.$

We also need to compute new limits:

| **$y$** | $3$ | $\frac{15}{4}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =\pi {\int }_{3}^{15/4}\sqrt{4y-11}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot {[\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(\sqrt{{4}^{3}}-\sqrt{{1}^{3}}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(8-1) \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093736/assets/21b55135fd1fbd0c3120b19ee6c4688dea2d8b13ccfe842e95262c87fb0bf6e0.png)

Consider the arc of the curve $y=-{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-4x$ that lies in the fourth quadrant between its $x$-intercepts. What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-4x & =0 \\ -x({x}^{2}-4x+4) & =0 \\ -x(x-2)^{2} & =0 \\ x & =0,2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=2.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-4x)=-3{x}^{2}+8x-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x\sqrt{1+{(-3{x}^{2}+8x-4)}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the arc of the curve $y=2x-{x}^{2}$ that lies in the first quadrant between its $x$-intercepts. What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ x(2-x) & =0 \\ x & =0,2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=2.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x-{x}^{2})=2-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x\sqrt{1+{(2-2x)}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x\sqrt{1+4-8x+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x\sqrt{5-8x+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $x=\sqrt{1-2y}$ that lies between the lines $y=-3$ and $y=0.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\sqrt{1-2y}) \\  & =\frac{-2}{2\sqrt{1-2y}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-2y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}=\frac{1}{1-2y}.
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-3}^{0}\sqrt{1-2y}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{1-2y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-3}^{0}\sqrt{1-2y}\sqrt{\frac{2-2y}{1-2y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\pi {\int }_{-3}^{0}\sqrt{1-y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\pi {[-\frac{2}{3}(1-y)^{3/2}]}_{-3}^{0} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\pi (-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{16}{3}) \\  & =\frac{28\sqrt{2}\,\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
